competitive_position: the company describes itself as the world's largest thin-film photovoltaic solar module manufacturer and the largest PV module manufacturer in the Western Hemisphere, having sold more than 40 GW-DC of modules cumulatively [c9].

Its modules use cadmium telluride (CdTe) semiconductor technology rather than the crystalline silicon used by most competitors; the company cites advantages in heat and humidity response, resistance to a type of physical cell cracking, a faster energy payback period of about four months, and a smaller manufacturing carbon and water footprint versus crystalline silicon [c9].
The company reported 17.5 gigawatts-DC of net bookings in 2021, including 11.8 gigawatts-DC booked since the Q3 2021 earnings call in early November [c7].

Planned capacity additions include a third U.S. manufacturing facility (3.3 GW-DC), targeted for the first half of 2023, and a first manufacturing facility in India (3.3 GW-DC), targeted for the second half of 2023 [c10].

United States sales represented 84% of 2021 net sales; India introduced a 40% import tariff on solar modules and 25% on solar cells effective April 2022, alongside a domestic-manufacturer preference policy for government-linked procurement [c11][c12].

Proposed U.S. federal legislation to incentivize domestic solar manufacturing was under discussion as of the filing date; the company stated it was unclear whether and to what extent such measures would be enacted [c16].

unresolved_questions: Does the lower 2022 guidance reflect a temporary cost and input-price squeeze, or a more structural pressure on module pricing and margins?
How will the new India tariffs and the pending, not-yet-enacted U.S. domestic-manufacturing incentive proposals affect the company's cost position versus crystalline-silicon competitors?
Will the $850M-$1.1B of planned 2022 capex be funded without new financing, given the guided net cash range and no disclosed dividend or buyback program?

macro_context.item: India import tariffs of 40% on solar modules and 25% on solar cells, effective April 2022
macro_context.business_connection: the company is building its first India manufacturing facility and sells into the Indian market, so India trade policy on solar equipment directly affects that plan

macro_context.item: Proposed but not-yet-enacted U.S. federal incentives for domestic solar manufacturing (tax credits, domestic content/labor requirements)
macro_context.business_connection: Would potentially benefit a U.S.-based module manufacturer such as the company if enacted, but the company itself described the outcome as uncertain

own: The low end of 2022 EPS guidance is $0.00, not negative, and the company still guides to a $1.1-1.35 billion year-end 2022 net cash balance [c6].
The company already had 17.5 GW-DC of 2021 net bookings, including 11.8 GW-DC booked since the Q3 call, which does not read as demand collapsing alongside this guidance cut [c7].

The new capacity (third U.S. plant, first India plant) follows two consecutive profitable years after a 2019 loss, and the higher 2022 capex is guided to be funded without a stated new financing need [c6][c15].
flat: The company explicitly attributes part of the 2022 gross-profit guidance to $10-15 million of underutilization losses tied to the capacity transition -- a cost tied to the buildout schedule rather than to end-market demand [c6].

FY2021 EPS of $4.38, while above the November 2021 guidance midpoint, was still within (not above) the original guidance range issued in February 2021 ($4.05-$4.75), suggesting cost pressure was already present during 2021 before the much larger 2022 guidance cut [c5].
short: The 2022 EPS guidance midpoint of about $0.30 is roughly 93% below the $4.38 actually earned in 2021 -- one of the largest guided profit declines disclosed in this release -- and planned 2022 capex of $850 million-$1.1 billion is roughly double 2021's actual spend, adding execution risk on two new facilities started at the same time [c6][c14][c10].

scene.question: Is a 90% guided profit drop a temporary squeeze while capacity is built, or a margin problem the bookings can't fix?

ask_friend.q: Why is next year's profit guided so low?
ask_friend.a: Guidance for 2022 is net sales of $2.4 to 2.6 billion, gross profit of $155 to 215 million and diluted EPS of $0.00 to 0.60, after $4.38 earned in 2021 [c6][c4]. The company's own explanation inside the release: $10 to 15 million of underutilisation losses tied to the capacity transition, freight and input costs, and a smaller sales volume while new plants are built [c6]. What the release does not contain is any guidance beyond 2022.

Not on the order book. 2021 net bookings were 17.5 GW-DC, 11.8 GW-DC of them since the third-quarter call, which is more than two years of the guided 2022 shipments [c7]. The plan is to double capacity: a third US plant for the first half of 2023 and a first Indian plant for the second half, with 2022 capex of $850 million to 1.1 billion, roughly double 2021 [c10][c6]. The United States was 84% of 2021 sales [c11]; India has just imposed 40% module tariffs [c12].

ask_friend.q: What is the stock already pricing?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $75.62, down 38% from the 12-month high and down 27% over three months. Market capitalisation is about $8.0 billion, or $6.5 billion after $1.6 billion of net cash, which is roughly 2.2 times 2021 revenue [c2]. The company guides to $1.1 to 1.35 billion of net cash at the end of 2022 even with the capex step-up [c6]. Note the company was loss-making as recently as 2019 [c15], and a US domestic-manufacturing incentive exists only as proposed legislation [c16].
